layers.arm_c_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020:
• GTAW: gas tungsten arc welding (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 69; Clause 4, p. 29) — Defined as: "An arc welding process using an arc between a tungsten electrode (nonconsumable) and the weld pool. • pulsed welding, arc welding (Clause 4, p. 46): "A process variation in which the welding power source output cycles between low and high power levels, resulting in a lower average power."

layers.arm_b_text:

• FRW: friction welding (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 27) — Defined as: "A solid-state welding process producing a weld under the compressive force contact of work- pieces rotating or moving relative to one another to produce heat and plastically displace material from the faying surfaces. See Figures B14(D), B23(I), B30(D), and B52. See also high-frequency seam welding and induction seam welding." question: What is the difference between FLSP, FLSP-P, and FLSP-W?
elements_present: A thermal spraying process in which an o
A flame spraying process variation in wh

layers.arm_b_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020:
• FLSP: flame spraying (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 25) — Defined as: "A thermal spraying process in which an oxyfuel gas flame is the source of heat for melting the surfacing material. Compressed gas may or may not be used for atomizing and propelling the surfacing material to the substrate."
• FLSP-P: powder flame spraying (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 44) — Defined as: "A flame spraying process variation in which the surfacing material is in powder form."
• FLSP-W: wire flame spraying (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 66) — Defined as: "A flame spraying process variation in which the surfacing material is in wire form."

Consumable Form and Process Hierarchy Distinction:
• FLSP (flame spraying) is the root thermal spraying process (Table A1, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 25) that can utilize surfacing material in either powder or wire form.
• FLSP-P (powder flame spraying, Clause 4, p. 44) is a standardized process variation specifically restricted to surfacing material in powder form.
• FLSP-W (wire flame spraying, Clause 4, p. 66) is a standardized process variation specifically restricted to surfacing material in wire form.

layers.arm_a_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020 Figure B23 (Welding Application Nomenclature, printed p.
layers.arm_b_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020 Figure B23 (Welding Application Nomenclature, printed p.
layers.arm_c_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020 Figure B23 (Welding Application Nomenclature, printed p. 116, PDF index 128), sub-diagram (J) TEMPER BEADS illustrates the placement of temper beads and toe temper beads in groove, fillet, and overlay welds.

Measurement of Distance S and Offset Dimension:
• Per Figure B23 Note (1): 'The distance, S, is measured from the toe of the weld to the edge of the temper beads. Measurements shall be made parallel to the base metal surface.'
• The specified offset dimension for the first layer temper beads is APPROX. 1 mm [0.040 in].
• General Notes:
  (a) Weld beads shown above may be deposited in any sequence that will result in placement of the beads as shown.
  (b) Surface temper reinforcing beads may cover the entire weld surface or may only be placed at the toe of the weld. They may or may not be mechanically removed.
  (2) Beads near the finished surface may be both tempering beads and surface temper reinforcing beads.

Clause 4 Definitions:
• temper pass (Clause 4, p. 58): "A weld pass used to modify the metallurgical properties of the heat-affected zone or previously deposited weld metal. The result of a temper pass is a temper bead. See Figure B23(J)."
• temper bead (Clause 4, p. 58): "A weld bead resulting from a temper pass. See also cosmetic bead, intermediate bead, and smoothing bead."
• temper bead sequence (Clause 4, p. 58): "A cross-sectional sequence in a multiple-pass weld in which the order and position of weld passes result in the creation of temper beads. See Figure B23(J)."
• toe temper pass (Clause 4, p. 60): "A weld pass applied to the cover bead adjacent to the weld toe in a manner to modify the metallurgical properties of the cover bead heat-affected zone. The result of a toe temper pass is a toe temper bead. See Figure B23(J)."
• toe temper bead (Clause 4, p. 59): "A weld bead resulting from a toe temper pass. See Figure B23(J)."

slice_name: Slice 16 — Suffix Modifiers, Appending Grammar & Mode Definitions
question: List all six application modes and their letter designation suffixes from Table A4, explain the rule and format for appending them to a process or process variation designation, and give the Clause 4 definitions that distinguish the six application modes.

layers.arm_a_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020 Table A4—Suffixes for Application Mode of Welding, Joining, and Allied Processes (Suffixes for Application Mode, printed p.
layers.arm_b_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020 Table A4—Suffixes for Application Mode of Welding, Joining, and Allied Processes (Suffixes for Application Mode, printed p.
layers.arm_c_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020 Table A4—Suffixes for Application Mode of Welding, Joining, and Allied Processes (Suffixes for Application Mode, printed p. 74), exactly six standardized letter designation suffixes are established:
- -AD = Adaptive control (Clause 4, p. 7): "Pertaining to process control, which senses changes in conditions and directs the equipment to take appropriate action. See Table A4. See also automatic, manual, mechanized, robotic, and semiautomatic."
- -AU = Automatic (Clause 4, p. 9): "Pertaining to process control with equipment requiring only occasional or no observation and no manual adjustments during its operation. See Table A4. See also adaptive control, manual, mechanized, robotic, and semiautomatic."
- -MA = Manual (Clause 4, p. 37): "Pertaining to the control of a process with the torch, gun, or electrode holder held and manipulated by hand. Accessory equipment, such as part motion devices and handheld material feeders may be used. See Table A4. See also adaptive control, automatic, mechanized, robotic, and semiautomatic."
- -ME = Mechanized (Clause 4, p. 38): "Pertaining to control of a process being mechanically moved along a preset path where manual adjustments may be made by an operator in response to visual observation of the process. See Table A4. See also adaptive control, automatic, manual, robotic, and semiautomatic."
- -RO = Robotic (Clause 4, p. 49): "Pertaining to process control with equipment moving along a controlled path using controlled parameters with no manual intervention once a cycle is initiated. See Table A4. See also adaptive control, automatic, manual, mechanized, and semiautomatic."
- -SA = Semiautomatic (Clause 4, p. 51): "Pertaining to the manual application of a process with equipment controlling one or more of the process conditions. See Table A4. See also adaptive control, automatic, manual, mechanized, and robotic."

Hyphenation Rule: Per Table A4 note and Annex C C1.3(5), Application mode designator is added to a process designator in the following format: XXXX-YY, where XXXX is the process designator and YY is the application mode designator. For example, manual gas tungsten arc welding is designated as GTAW-MA. Suffixes are appended in the format XXXX-YY, where XXXX is the process letter designation and YY is the application mode suffix (e.g. GTAW-MA, GMAW-SA, SAW-AU).

slice_name: Slice 17 — Multi-Family Process Decoding & Vacuum Pressure Limits
question: Decode the letter designations LBC, LBC-A, LBC-EV, LBC-IG, LBC-O and EBW, EBW-HV, EBW-MV, EBW-NV from Annex A (Tables A1–A3), and state how Clause 4 defines each variation, including the exact operating pressure ranges in pascals and torr for the electron beam welding variations.
elements_present: A thermal cutting process severing metal
laser beam air cutting, laser beam evaporative cutting, laser beam inert gas cutting, and laser beam  oxygen cutting
A laser beam cutting process variation m
A laser beam cutting process variation v
A laser beam cutting process variation u
high vacuum electron beam welding, medium vacuum electron beam welding,  and nonvacuum electron beam welding
An electron beam welding process variati

layers.arm_c_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020:
• LBC: laser beam cutting (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 35) — Defined as: "A thermal cutting process severing metal by locally melting or vaporizing it with the heat from a laser beam. The process is used with or without assist gas to aid the removal of molten and vaporized material. See also laser beam air cutting, laser beam evaporative cutting, laser beam inert gas cutting, and laser beam oxygen cutting."
• LBC-A: laser beam air cutting (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 35) — Defined as: "A laser beam cutting process variation melting the workpiece and using an air jet to remove molten and vaporized material."
• LBC-EV: laser beam evaporative cutting (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 35) — Defined as: "A laser beam cutting process variation vaporizing the workpiece, with or without an assist gas, typically inert gas, to aid the removal of vaporized material."
• LBC-IG: laser beam inert gas cutting (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 36) — Defined as: "A laser beam cutting process variation melting the workpiece and using an inert assist gas to remove molten and vaporized material."
• LBC-O: laser beam oxygen cutting (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 70; Clause 4, p. 36) — Defined as: "A laser beam cutting process variation using heat from the chemical reaction between oxygen and the base metal at elevated temperatures. The necessary temperature is maintained with a laser beam."
• EBW: electron beam welding (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 69; Clause 4, p. 23) — Defined as: "A welding process producing coalescence with a concentrated beam, composed prima- rily of high-velocity electrons, impinging on the joint. The process is used without shielding gas and without the application of pressure. See also high vacuum electron beam welding, medium vacuum electron beam welding, and nonvacuum electron beam welding."
• EBW-HV: high vacuum electron beam welding (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 69; Clause 4, p. 31) — Defined as: "An electron beam welding process variation in which welding is accomplished at a pressure of 10–4 to 10–1 pascals [approximately 10–6 to 10–3 torr]."
• EBW-MV: medium vacuum electron beam welding (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 69; Clause 4, p. 38) — Defined as: "An electron beam welding process variation in which welding is accomplished at a pressure of 10–1 pascal to 3 × 103 pascal [approximately 10–3 torr to 25 torr]."
• EBW-NV: nonvacuum electron beam welding (Table A1/A2/A3/A5, p. 69; Clause 4, p. 40) — Defined as: "An electron beam welding process variation in which welding is accomplished at atmospheric pressure."

Physical operating pressure ranges distinguishing EBW process variations:
1. EBW-HV (High vacuum electron beam welding, Clause 4 p. 31): Operates at high vacuum pressures, specifically: "An electron beam welding process variation in which welding is accomplished at a pressure of 10–4 to 10–1 pascals [approximately 10–6 to 10–3 torr]." (10^-4 to 10^-1 Pa [10^-6 to 10^-3 Torr])
2. EBW-MV (Medium vacuum electron beam welding, Clause 4 p. 38): Operates at medium vacuum pressures, specifically: "An electron beam welding process variation in which welding is accomplished at a pressure of 10–1 pascal to 3 × 103 pascal [approximately 10–3 torr to 25 torr]." (0.1 to 100 Pa [10^-3 to 1 Torr])
3. EBW-NV (Nonvacuum electron beam welding, Clause 4 p. 40): Operates at atmospheric pressure, specifically: "An electron beam welding process variation in which welding is accomplished at atmospheric pressure."

slice_name: Slice 18 — Personal Safety Exception & Nonstandard/Incorrect Terms
question: According to the Foreword and Annex C, under what specific exception does AWS A3.0 classify a term as both "nonstandard and incorrect"? Identify the electrical circuit terms in Clause 4 that carry this "nonstandard and incorrect" designation, and provide the definitions of the standard terms that must be used instead (including the safety distinction with ground connection in Figure B34).

layers.arm_a_text: Per Annex C Clause C2.3 (printed p.
layers.arm_b_text: Per Annex C Clause C2.3 (printed p.
layers.arm_c_text:
Per Annex C Clause C2.3 (printed p. 163, PDF index 175) and the Foreword of AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020: Terms are categorized as either standard or nonstandard. No other designation, such as preferred or nonpreferred, acceptable or nonacceptable, correct or incorrect is used, EXCEPT that when the misuse of a term may endanger personal safety, the term is identified as both 'nonstandard and incorrect' (Example: ground lead).

Electrical Circuit Terms Designated as 'Nonstandard and Incorrect' (or 'Incorrect') in Clause 4:
• ground clamp (Clause 4, p. 29): "A nonstandard and incorrect term for workpiece connection." — Standard term: workpiece connection
• ground lead (Clause 4, p. 30): "A nonstandard and incorrect term for workpiece lead." — Standard term: workpiece lead
• welding ground (Clause 4, p. 65): "A nonstandard and incorrect term for workpiece connection." — Standard term: workpiece connection
• silver soldering (Clause 4, p. 52): "An incorrect term for brazing with a silver-containing brazing filler metal." — Standard term: brazing with a silver filler metal

Standard Terminology and Safety Distinction (Figure B34, printed p. 140, PDF index 152):
In Figure B34 (Welding Current Polarity), AWS A3.0 emphasizes that 'ground connection' connects the welding machine frame to earth potential solely for personnel safety against electric shock. In contrast, welding current returns through the 'workpiece lead' attached via the 'workpiece connection' (or 'workpiece connector'). Referring to the workpiece lead or connection as a 'ground lead' or 'ground clamp' is hazardous because it obscures this vital life-safety electrical distinction.

Standard Terms to be Used Instead:
• workpiece connection (Clause 4, p. 67): "A nonstandard term when used for workpiece connector."
• workpiece connector (Clause 4, p. 67): "A device used to provide an electrical connection between the workpiece and the workpiece lead. See Figure B34."
• workpiece lead (Clause 4, p. 67): "A secondary circuit conductor transmitting energy from the power source to the workpiece connector. See Figure B34."
• electrode lead (Clause 4, p. 22): "A secondary circuit conductor transmitting energy from the power source to the electrode holder, gun, or torch. See Figures B34 and B36."
• ground connection (Clause 4, p. 30): "An electrical connection of the welding machine frame to the earth for safety. See Figure B34. See also workpiece connection and workpiece lead. ground lead. A nonstandard and incorrect term for workpiece lead."

slice_name: Slice 19 — Edition Revision Decisions & Normative Rationale
question: Explain two major terminology revisions documented in Annex C (Clauses C1.5.6 and C1.5.7) and Annex D of AWS A3.0:2020: (1) Why was parallel joint introduced to replace edge joint among the five basic joint types, and how are both terms defined in Clause 4? (2) How did the 13th edition change the status of nondestructive evaluation, nondestructive inspection (NDI), and nondestructive testing (NDT) relative to nondestructive examination (NDE), and why was the definition of nondestructive examination (NDE) itself modified?
elements_present: butt, corner, lap, parallel, and T-joints
determining acceptability of a material or a component in accordance with established criteria without impairing its future usefulness

layers.arm_a_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020, two major terminology revisions are documented in Annex C (Clauses C1.5.6 and C1.5.7) and Annex D:
layers.arm_b_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020, two major terminology revisions are documented in Annex C (Clauses C1.5.6 and C1.5.7) and Annex D:
layers.arm_c_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020, two major terminology revisions are documented in Annex C (Clauses C1.5.6 and C1.5.7) and Annex D:

1. Introduction of 'parallel joint' replacing 'edge joint' (Clause C1.5.7, printed p. 162):
   • Rationale: Historically, five basic joint types were recognized (butt, corner, edge, lap, T-joint). The names of four described member orientation, but 'edge joint' identified weld location rather than member orientation and conflicted with 'edge weld'. To eliminate this irregularity, 'parallel joint' was introduced as a replacement among the five basic joint types: butt, corner, lap, parallel, and T-joints. Edge joint was retained as a standard cross-reference ('See parallel joint').
   • Annex D Classification: 'parallel joint' is added in Table D1 (New Terms, p. 165), while 'joint type' and 'edge joint' are listed in Table D2 (Substantially Revised, p. 169).

2. Elevation of NDE Alternatives & Revised Definition of NDE (Clause C1.5.6, printed pp. 161–162):
   • Rationale: In the 2001 edition, nondestructive examination (NDE) was chosen as the standard term, and evaluation, inspection, and testing were listed as nonstandard. In the 13th edition (2020), because all four terms are widely used across standards bodies (ASME, ASNT, ASTM) and industry, the committee recognized evaluation, inspection (NDI), and testing (NDT) as valid standard alternatives directing to NDE ('See nondestructive examination').
   • Definition Revision: The definition of nondestructive examination (NDE) itself was revised because performing NDE cannot guarantee 'suitability for its intended purpose'; it was changed to: 'The process of determining acceptability of a material or a component in accordance with established criteria without impairing its future usefulness.'
   • Annex D Classification: Table D5 (Terms Revised from Nonstandard to Standard, p. 170) records nondestructive evaluation, nondestructive inspection (NDI), and nondestructive testing (NDT). Table D2 lists the revised definition of nondestructive examination (NDE).

Verbatim Clause 4 Definitions:
• joint (Clause 4, p. 34): "The junction of workpiece(s) before and after joining. See Figures B1 and B2."
• joint type (Clause 4, p. 34): "Classification of a joint based upon the relative orientation of the workpieces being joined. See Figures B1 and B2. See butt joint, corner joint, parallel joint, flanged butt joint, flanged corner joint, flanged parallel joint, flanged lap joint, flanged T-joint, lap joint, and T-joint."
• parallel joint (Clause 4, p. 42): "A joint type formed by butting, parallel surfaces of one or more workpieces with flush ends. See Figures B1(E) and B2(E). See also skewed joint."
• edge joint (Clause 4, p. 21): "See parallel joint."
• nondestructive examination (Clause 4, p. 40): "(NDE). The process of determining acceptability of a material or a component in accord- ance with established criteria without impairing its future usefulness."
• nondestructive evaluation (Clause 4, p. 40): "See nondestructive examination."
• nondestructive inspection (Clause 4, p. 40): "(NDI). See nondestructive examination."
• nondestructive testing (Clause 4, p. 40): "(NDT). See nondestructive examination."

slice_name: Slice 20 — Dual Waveform Comparison & 11 Cycle Interval Definitions
question: Compare the resistance spot welding waveforms in Figure B49 (Pulsation Welding Waveform) and Figure B50 (Single-Pulse Resistance Spot Welding Waveform): how does Clause 4 distinguish weld time, resistance welding from weld interval, resistance welding, and cool time, resistance welding from quench time, resistance welding? Additionally, define the sequential cycle intervals shown across Figures B49 and B50: squeeze time, preweld interval, preheat time, upslope time, pulse time, downslope time, temper time, hold time, postweld interval, forge-delay time, and off time.

layers.arm_a_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020, Figure B49 (Example of a Pulsation Welding Waveform for Resistance Spot Welding) and Figure B50 (Example of a Single-Pulse Resistance Spot Welding Waveform) share printed p.
layers.arm_b_text: In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020, Figure B49 (Example of a Pulsation Welding Waveform for Resistance Spot Welding) and Figure B50 (Example of a Single-Pulse Resistance Spot Welding Waveform) share printed p.
layers.arm_c_text:
In AWS A3.0M/A3.0:2020, Figure B49 (Example of a Pulsation Welding Waveform for Resistance Spot Welding) and Figure B50 (Example of a Single-Pulse Resistance Spot Welding Waveform) share printed p. 153 (PDF index 165).

Key Distinctions in Clause 4:
1. weld time vs. weld interval:
   • 'weld time, resistance welding': The duration for which welding current is applied to the workpiece in making a weld without pulsation (single-pulse), or during each heat time in pulsation welding.
   • 'weld interval, resistance welding': The total elapsed time of the welding current including heat times and cool times in multiple-impulse or pulsation resistance welding.
2. cool time vs. quench time:
   • 'cool time, resistance welding': The duration between successive heat times in multiple-impulse or pulsation resistance welding.
   • 'quench time, resistance welding': The duration from the end of the weld interval to the beginning of the temper time.

Definitions of Sequential Cycle Intervals across Figures B49 and B50:
• squeeze time (Clause 4, p. 55): "The interval between initiation of the welding cycle and first application of current. See Figures B49 and B50."
• preweld interval (Clause 4, p. 45): "The elapsed time between the initiation of the squeeze time and the beginning of the weld time or weld interval time. See Figure B50."
• preheat time (Clause 4, p. 45): "The duration of preheat current flow. See Figure B49."
• upslope time (Clause 4, p. 61): "The interval during which the welding current or power is continuously increased. See Figures B49 and B53."
• weld time (Clause 4, p. 64): "resistance welding. The duration of time when welding current passes through workpieces in a single pulse. See Figures B49 and B50. See also weld interval."
• weld interval (Clause 4, p. 63): "The sum of heat and cool times to produce a pulsation weld. See Figure B49. See also weld time."
• heat time (Clause 4, p. 30): "See weld time."
• cool time (Clause 4, p. 17): "Any interval between squeeze time and hold time when no resistance welding current is being conducted. See Figure B49."
• pulse time (Clause 4, p. 46): "The duration of a pulse. See Figure B49 and B50."
• downslope time (Clause 4, p. 21): "The interval during which the welding current or power is continuously decreased. See Figures B49 and B53."
• quench time (Clause 4, p. 47): "The duration from the end of the weld interval or downslope time to the beginning of the temper time, during which no current flows through the workpieces and the weld is rapidly cooled by the electrodes. See Figure B49."
• temper time (Clause 4, p. 58): "The time following quench time during which a current is passed through the weld for heat treating. See Figure B49."
• hold time (Clause 4, p. 31): "The duration of force application after the last heat function has ended. See Figures B49 and B51."
• postweld interval (Clause 4, p. 44): "The duration from the end of the weld interval through the hold time. See Figure B49."
• forge-delay time (Clause 4, p. 27): "The duration between a preselected point in the welding cycle and the initiation of the forging force. See Figure B49."
• off time (Clause 4, p. 40): "The interval between welding cycles when operating in a repeat mode. See Figure B50."
